meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Do one thing every day that scares you'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Eleanor Roosevelt. The exact wording was written by columnist Mary Schmich in her 1997 Chicago Tribune "Sunscreen" essay.

answer.label: Not Eleanor Roosevelt — written by Mary Schmich
answer.authorDates: b. 1953 · Pulitzer-winning Chicago Tribune columnist; wrote the line in 1997
answer.sourceLine: The exact sentence first appears in Mary Schmich’s 1 June 1997 Chicago Tribune column (later famous as the “Wear Sunscreen” essay). No documented source shows Eleanor Roosevelt ever said or wrote it — Schmich herself has said she has found no such evidence.

source.excerpt: Do one thing every day that scares you.
trail: 1 June 1997 — the exact sentence appears in Mary Schmich’s Chicago Tribune column, per Quote Investigator ↗.
By 2008 the line is printed in Meg Cabot’s The Princess Diaries, Volume IX: Princess Mia credited to Eleanor Roosevelt — an early vector for the misattribution, documented by QI ↗.
Today it is routinely tagged to Eleanor Roosevelt on aggregators like Goodreads ↗, which notes such quotes are community-added and unverified.
source.cutTag: ↑ one line from a long list of playful graduation advice
source.excerptNote: The line runs as one beat in Schmich’s staccato list of mock-commencement advice — the same column that opens “Wear sunscreen.” It was written as a hypothetical graduation speech she would give “if I could.”
source.rightsNote: The quote is not public domain: it is a line from a 1997 newspaper column, in copyright to Mary Schmich / the Chicago Tribune. Reproduce with attribution.

author.name: Mary Schmich
author.heading: Mary Schmich
author.bio: Mary Schmich is an American journalist who wrote a metro column for the Chicago Tribune for decades and won the 2012 Pulitzer Prize for Commentary. Her 1 June 1997 column — a tongue-in-cheek graduation speech beginning “Wear sunscreen” — became a global phenomenon after Baz Luhrmann set it to music in 1999. Its individual lines, including “Do one thing every day that scares you,” have since drifted loose and been re-credited to more famous names.

misattribution.heading: Why Eleanor Roosevelt gets the credit
misattribution.intro: The sentence is one of the most confidently misattributed lines on the internet. The real author is alive and has publicly disowned the Roosevelt credit.

items.why: No speech, book, column, or letter by Roosevelt has ever been found containing the line. Quote Investigator ↗ notes the earliest exact match is Schmich in 1997 — decades after Roosevelt’s death in 1962 — and that Schmich herself said in 2012 she had seen no evidence Roosevelt said it. Roosevelt’s actual nearby line, from You Learn by Living (1960), is the different “You must do the thing you think you cannot do.”
When Schmich’s column went viral by email in August 1997, it was falsely passed around as a Kurt Vonnegut MIT commencement address — a myth recounted by QI ↗. Vonnegut never gave that speech.

misattribution.truthLine: The exact wording is Mary Schmich’s, first printed in her 1 June 1997 Chicago Tribune column, per Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: An older family of the same idea
lead: The sentiment is far older than 1997, which is part of why a grande dame like Eleanor Roosevelt feels like a plausible source. A whole family of “do the thing you fear” sayings runs back through the 20th and 19th centuries.

Ralph Waldo Emerson wrote “Always do what you are afraid to do” in his 1841 essay Heroism, and Roosevelt’s own 1960 “You must do the thing you think you cannot do” sits squarely in the same tradition. But a shared theme is not the same as authorship of a specific sentence.
detailsBody: Misattribution tends to flow uphill toward fame: an anonymous or lesser-known author’s line gets reassigned to whoever sounds most quotable. Roosevelt, a byword for courage, is a magnet for courage quotes. Once a line appears in a printed book (here, a 2008 novel) with the wrong name, aggregators copy it and the error hardens.
context.pull: Same idea for 150 years — but this exact sentence is Schmich’s, 1997.
